ControlEvent.description:
What the host sends on an authorised control stream outside a response.

The control stream carries ordinary [`Notification`] events once the connection is authorised.
These two messages are the connection's own, not an application event: the freshness resource
and the transport's liveness belong to the connection rather than to any session.

oneOf.description:
The host renewed this connection's action window.

Section 9: windows are short-lived freshness resources, renewed explicitly on a live
authorised connection. The host renews on its own schedule, so a client never has to ask
for one and never has to guess how long it has.

A keepalive. It carries nothing; its arrival is the whole message.

Section 23 puts the keepalive at ten seconds while active and the inactivity threshold at
30. The transport's own keepalive covers a network connection; this one also covers a local
socket, which carries the same typed frames and has no equivalent underneath it.

ControlFrame.description:
One frame on an authorised control stream.

The union is closed. A receiver that cannot name the variant rejects the frame rather than
guessing, which is what keeps an unknown method a correlated error instead of a parse failure.

Both transports carry these frames: section 23 says local Unix sockets and Windows named pipes
carry the same typed frames with local peer authentication. What differs is how the connection
is authenticated before the first frame, not what travels afterwards. One union rather than two
is what makes that true rather than merely stated: a request, a mutation, a response, a receipt
and a notification are the same types on a Unix socket as on a QUIC stream, and a host that
answered them differently would have two wire contracts to keep in step.

Some variants only ever travel between host processes on a local endpoint: the local opening
frames, the worker startup handshake, the generation and revision exchange, and a forwarded
mutation. They are still part of this union, because a closed union is what makes a frame that
does not belong on the ingress it arrived on a *refusal* rather than a parse failure. Each
endpoint refuses the variants its role does not serve, which is an admission rule the host
applies rather than a shape the wire hides.

ForwardedRequest.description:
A read the host admitted for a caller, passed to the component that owns its subject.

A read needs forwarding for the same reason a mutation does, and for one reason more. The
subject is the worker's, and the daemon owns admission; but a read is also *attributed*: the
de-duplication key of a retained receipt is the verified actor and the action together, so a
read that asks about an action has to ask as the caller rather than as the proxy. A plain
request carries no actor, and serving one on the proxy's own principal would answer about the
proxy's actions instead of the caller's.

What travels beside the request is the actor the host verified, including the ingress it
arrived on. The worker checks the method against *that* ingress, so a method the registry keeps
to private IPC stays unreachable for a paired device even though the frame arrived on a socket.

actor.description: The actor the host verified, with the ingress it arrived on.

authority_deadline_boot_ms.description:
When the authority behind this request runs out, on the machine's own continuous clock.

A read is not a mutation and carries no accepted deadline, but the authority behind it
still ends: a grant expires while the request is in the worker's queue, and raw input is a
request. The worker compares this inside the boundary that decides what reaches the
application, so bytes admitted a moment before an expiry are not written after it. Null
when the caller's authority is not something that expires, which is what a locally
authenticated caller's operating-system identity is.

InclusionChoice.description:
What a workspace does with the user's uncommitted work.

Every member is a decision the user made, and none of them removes anything from the user's own
tree: an exclusion means the new workspace starts without that file, never that the file is
cleaned, stashed or discarded where it is.

A shared workspace is not a sandbox; a worktree shares repository metadata; a working tree

MailboxPayloadType.description:

The set is closed. A new payload kind is a new schema, not a new string a sender may invent:
section 23 forbids unknown fields and strip-and-verify behaviour on signed objects, and the
same rule applies to the type that decides how a payload is interpreted.

has its own retention and is not coalesced with notifications; a device that sees this

A receipt for one action the host admitted, dispatched or refused.

It records what happened; it asks for nothing. An action reaches a host over its
authenticated connection and comes back with a receipt, and this is how that receipt reaches
a device that was not connected at the time.

that holds it. It is the repeated kind, so it is the one coalescing is mostly about.

authority revision record.

The payload is the signed object's canonical bytes. The issuer's signature is what
authorises it; the envelope only delivers it.

it is delivered, so which boundary counts decides what the payer pays for.

authorisation does. At renewal it goes straight to the host, in the answer to the renewal the

It grants delivery to one destination and nothing else: it is not a session, it reads nothing,
and it cannot be presented to any other method.

The host writes the underlying event first and then sends this, so a notification that is never
delivered has already been recorded somewhere the person can find it.

Nothing here is a field for plaintext that describes the work. The alert comes from a closed
vocabulary, the two identifiers are 128-bit values rather than text, and the preview is a sealed
envelope whose shape [`PushDeliveryRequest::preview_is_well_formed`] checks. Those are the
checks a gateway can make. What they do not do is inspect a producer: a host that put meaning
into its own identifiers, or sealed the wrong thing, has disclosed it to the provider and to the
gateway. Keeping the identifiers meaningless and the preview correctly sealed is the producer's
obligation, and section 16 places it there.

Larger detail does not belong here. Section 16 bounds the preview plaintext to
[`MAX_PREVIEW_PLAINTEXT_BYTES`] and the complete provider payload to
[`MAX_PROVIDER_PAYLOAD_BYTES`], and says to move the excess into a referenced encrypted object
rather than trusting an expansion ratio.

by the time it is tried again, as `token_disabled` or `refused` when the provider rejects
the token or the message, as `revoked` when the authorisation ends first, as `abandoned`
when the gateway stops trying, and as `expired` when the notification's moment passes.

The same request presented again while the gateway is still holding it is answered

decided is answered `duplicate`.

PushInstallationBinding.description:
The canonical active binding of one provider token to one installation.

There is exactly one of these per token digest. That is what stops an installation from
registering the same token under a second identity to start its rate history again: a second
identity for one token is not an additional binding, it is a replacement, and a replacement has
to pass its own challenge. The rate history stays with the digest through that replacement, so
the alias gains nothing.

The token itself is not here. The gateway keeps it where it keeps its own secrets, because it
needs the token to deliver; what travels in a record is the digest.

bound_at_ms.description: When the answered challenge bound it, in UTC milliseconds.

installation_id.description: The installation the token delivers to.

installation_key.description: The public key that installation authenticates with.

platform.description: The platform the token belongs to.

registration_id.description: The attempt whose answer established it.

state.description: Whether the provider still delivers to the token.

token_digest.description: The token, as the gateway records it.

PushPlatform.description:
A push platform, as the gateway builds a payload for it.

Both go through FCM HTTP v1. The distinction is the payload: an iOS message carries the APNs
alert, `mutable-content`, expiry and collapse headers the notification extension needs, and
Firebase forwards it through APNs with KalaReach's registered key and app topic.

oneOf.description: Android, through FCM directly.
iOS, through FCM to APNs.

PushPlatformHints.description: What the gateway asks each platform for, beyond the payload itself.

PushRatePolicy.description:
What a destination may receive, and how excess collapses.

Free push has its own budget and is never charged against a voice balance (section 17). The
policy is fixed when an authorisation is issued and a renewal cannot change it, so a host
cannot widen its own allowance by renewing.

burst.description: How many notifications may arrive in a burst.

collapse_window_ms.description: How often excess collapses into one attention update.

sustained_per_hour.description: How many may arrive in one hour.

PushRegistrationAnswer.description:
The receiver's answer to a challenge, signed by the proposed installation key.

The receiver answers only for its own locally pending registration and its own public key. It
does not sign a challenge that names an attempt it did not start, or an installation identifier
that is not the one its key derives, so a challenge aimed at a token in the hope of a reply gets
none.

installation_key.description: The public half of the key that answered. Its SHA-256 names the installation.

signature.description: The signature over [`PushRegistrationAnswerPayload::signing_input`].

PushRegistrationAnswerPayload.description:
What a registration answer states, and exactly what its signature covers.

Every field of the challenge is repeated here and covered by the signature, so an answer is a
statement about one attempt, one token and one gateway. Dropping any of them would let an answer
collected in one context be presented in another: without the token digest an answer would
activate a token nobody proved receipt of; without the origin it would answer a different
deployment's challenge; without the registration identifier it would complete whichever attempt
happened to be pending.

challenge.description: The value that arrived through the provider.

expires_at_ms.description: The expiry the challenge carried.

gateway_origin.description: The gateway that issued the challenge.

installation_id.description: The installation the answering key names.

platform.description: The platform the token belongs to.

token_digest.description: The token the challenge was sent to.

PushRegistrationChallenge.description:
The challenge the gateway sends through the provider to a proposed token.

It goes to the token, not to the caller. That is the whole point: an authenticated HTTP request
proves the caller holds an installation key, and nothing more. Sending a random value to the
token and requiring it back signed proves that the installation which holds the key is also the
one the provider delivers that token to. Until that returns, the registration stays pending and
no sender credential is issued.

The challenge is single use. An answer consumes it, and a second answer, whether the same one
replayed or another arriving at the same moment, finds nothing pending to answer.

challenge.description: The single-use random value the receiver returns.

expires_at_ms.description: When it stops being answerable, at most [`REGISTRATION_CHALLENGE_LIFETIME_MS`] after issue.

installation_id.description: The installation the pending registration is for.

platform.description: The platform the token belongs to.

registration_id.description: This attempt, so an answer cannot complete a different one.

token_digest.description: The token the challenge was sent to.

PushRegistrationId.description: One attempt to bind a push token to an installation. 128 random bits.

PushRegistrationProposal.description:
What a caller sends to begin a registration.

It proposes a token. It establishes nothing: the gateway records the attempt, sends a challenge
through the provider to that token, and waits. A caller that never receives the challenge has
only ever had a pending registration.

installation_key.description: The public key the installation will authenticate with. Its SHA-256 names the installation.

platform.description:
The platform whose payload the gateway should build for this token.

It is a claim, not a proof: receiving the challenge says the token reaches this device and
nothing about the label beside it. The gateway records it as delivery metadata and never
indexes by it.

registration_id.description: This attempt. A retry carrying the same value is the same attempt.

oneOf.description: Propose a token and ask for the challenge to be sent to it.

proposal.description: The token and the identity proposed for it.

oneOf.description: Present the challenge, signed, and activate the binding.

PushRequest.description:
Every body a signed push method carries.

One type, so there is one rule for what a service-request signature covers: the signature's
`body_digest` is [`PushRequest::digest`], and the method it names is [`PushRequest::method`]. A
body built for one method therefore cannot be presented under another, because the signature
covers both the body and the method and a verifier checks that they agree.

Delivery is not here. It carries the bearer credential the host was issued rather than a
signature, so it has no body digest to cover.

oneOf.description: `push.installation.register`.
`push.sender.issue`.
`push.sender.renew`.

request.description: The nonce request or the proof.

oneOf.description: `push.sender.revoke`.

request.description: The nonce request or the statement.

oneOf.description: The device and the host were unpaired.
The host replaced its signing key, which needs a new authorisation from the installation.
The installation replaced its own key, which revokes every authorisation it had given.

PushSenderBinding.description:
What one sender authorisation fixes for its lifetime.

A renewal proves the host is still there; it is not an opportunity to change what was
authorised. Every field a renewal must not touch is here and nowhere else, so
[`PushSenderRecord::renewal_preserves_binding`] is a comparison of one digest rather than a list
of fields somebody has to remember to extend.

host_endpoint_key.description: The host's iroh endpoint identity, so the installation knows which peer it authorised.

host_signing_key.description: The host's Ed25519 signing key. Renewal and revocation are proven with it.

PushSenderIssueRequest.description:
What an installation sends for `push.sender.issue`.

It names one paired host by both of its keys and asks for a credential scoped to that host and
this installation. The gateway sets the rate policy; a caller cannot ask for a wider one.

host_signing_key.description: The host's Ed25519 signing key, which will prove its renewals and its revocation.

sender_record_id.description: The authorisation being created. A retry carrying the same value is the same authorisation.

PushSenderNonceRequest.description: What a host sends to ask for the nonce its proof will answer.

sender_record_id.description: The authorisation the host is about to renew or revoke.

PushSenderRecord.description:
One installation's authorisation of one host, as the gateway holds it.

The authorisation and the credential have different lifetimes on purpose. The authorisation is
the installation's decision and lasts until the installation revokes it. The credential is a
bearer token that a host keeps on disk, so it expires in thirty days and is renewed by proving
possession of the key the installation named. An offline host that comes back after its
credential expired still renews, because what it proves has not lapsed.

binding.description: What the installation authorised, and what a renewal may not change.

credential_expires_at_ms.description: When the current credential stops working.

issued_at_ms.description: When the installation authorised the host, in UTC milliseconds.

revision.description: The gateway's revision, advanced on every renewal.

state.description: Whether the authorisation still stands.

PushSenderRecordId.description: One installation's authorisation of one paired host to send it notifications.

PushSenderRenewRequest.description:
What a host sends for `push.sender.renew`.

Two steps, because the proof answers a nonce the gateway chose. The first asks for the nonce and
the second returns it signed, so a captured renewal answers a question that has already been
asked and closed.

oneOf.description: Ask for a fresh nonce to renew against.
Present the renewal proof and take the new credential.

PushSenderRenewal.description: A host's proof that it still holds the key the installation authorised.

signature.description: The host signing key's signature over [`PushSenderRenewalPayload::signing_input`].

PushSenderRenewalPayload.description:
What a renewal proof states, and exactly what its signature covers.

The nonce is the gateway's, handed out for this renewal and accepted once. Without it a captured
renewal would be usable for as long as the host key lived; with it, a renewal is a reply to a
question the gateway asked a moment ago.

gateway_nonce.description: The single-use value the gateway handed out for this renewal.

gateway_origin.description: The gateway that issued the nonce.

requested_at_ms.description: When the host signed, in UTC milliseconds.

PushSenderRevision.description: The revision of one push sender record, advanced by the gateway on every renewal.

PushSenderRevocation.description: A host's statement that an authorisation is finished.

signature.description: The host signing key's signature over [`PushSenderRevocationPayload::signing_input`].

PushSenderRevocationPayload.description: What a revocation states, and exactly what its signature covers.

gateway_nonce.description: The single-use value the gateway handed out for this revocation.

gateway_origin.description: The gateway that issued the nonce.

requested_at_ms.description: When the host signed, in UTC milliseconds.

oneOf.description: Ask for a fresh nonce to revoke against.
Present the revocation and end the authorisation.

PushSenderState.description: Whether a sender authorisation still stands.

oneOf.description: The installation's authorisation stands. The credential may be renewed.

It was revoked, by unpairing or by the installation key being replaced.

A revoked record never becomes active again. A host that needs to send after this needs a
new authorisation from the installation, which is a decision made on the device.

PushSuppression.description:
What the gateway suppressed, so the host can record it.

The host retains every request it made and reports suppression locally, which is what keeps a
suppressed notification from becoming a lost decision: the pending work is still on the host and
still visible there.

collapsed_into.description: The attention update this collapsed into.

next_update_at_ms.description: When the next attention update may be sent, in UTC milliseconds.

suppressed_count.description: How many notifications have collapsed into the current update, including this one.

PushSuppressionReason.description: Why a notification was suppressed, when it was.

oneOf.description: The burst allowance was spent.
The hourly allowance was spent.

PushTokenState.description: Whether a bound token is still usable.

oneOf.description: The provider delivers to it.

The provider rejected it as unregistered or invalid.

Nothing is sent to a disabled token. Only a fresh native registration, which proves receipt
again, puts a token back in service; a host cannot re-enable one by asking.

PushUrgency.description: How urgently a provider is asked to deliver.

oneOf.description: Deliver now: a person is waiting. FCM `high`, APNs priority 10.
Deliver when convenient. FCM `normal`, APNs priority 5.

QuestionRevision.description: The exact version of a question that a person answers.

QueueDrainReport.description:
Which of the reader's input queues the bridge has cleared.

A fence publishes only when all three are clear. Reporting them separately is what makes a
retry possible: the worker learns which queue is still holding input rather than only that the
transition failed.

tty_typeahead_drained.description: The terminal's typeahead has been consumed by this reader.

ReaderContext.description:
Which reader a root editor event belongs to.

The three are what a pre-EOF decision and a fence acknowledgement have to distinguish. Only the
primary reader can carry the empty-prompt detach; a continuation line and the `read` builtin are
ordinary input even when the buffer looks empty.

oneOf.description: The primary prompt of the managed root editor.
A continuation line of an unfinished command.
The shell's `read` builtin reading through the line editor.

ReaderRevision.description: The revision of the reader inside one prompt. It advances whenever the reader restarts or is replaced.

Receipt.description:
One action receipt.

The de-duplication key is `(actor_id, action_id)`. An exact duplicate returns the stored
receipt; a reused identifier with a different payload digest is an `ID_CONFLICT`.

accepted_deadline_ms.description:
The deadline the host derived at acceptance: the earliest of window expiry, receipt time
plus the requested time to live, and any applicable authority or subject deadline. An exact
retry never receives a new deadline.

actor_id.description: The verified actor that submitted it.

error.description: The failure recorded with a refusal, rejection or unknown outcome.

method.description: The method and version the digest covers.

method_version.description: The method version the digest covers.

payload_digest.description: The digest of the submitted payload, used to detect a reused identifier.

reason.description: Why the action was rejected, when the state is `rejected`.

state.description: The current state.

ReceiptResponse.description:
The response to a mutation request.

A duplicate request from a still-authorised actor returns the retained receipt without
dispatch. The host checks current authority before returning it, so a revoked device cannot use
an old action identifier to retrieve protected information.

request_id.description: The request this response correlates with.

ReceiptState.description: The state of one action receipt.

oneOf.description: The connection acknowledged the request. Transient, never durable acceptance.
The intent is durably committed. No dispatch marker exists yet.
A durable dispatch marker was committed before crossing the external-effect boundary.

The authoritative interface acknowledged the operation. Terminal for admission and
dispatch; later work completion is separate evidence.

The authoritative interface proved the operation was refused without the requested effect.
Terminal. This is not a local pre-dispatch rejection.

Never dispatched. Admission failure, or later expiry, cancellation, revocation or stale
preconditions before dispatch. Terminal.

Dispatch may have occurred. This identifier is never dispatched again. Later authoritative
reconciliation may move it to applied or refused; otherwise it stays unknown.

ReceiveLimits.description:
The receive limits a peer declares.

Both sides state their own bounds; the selection carries the negotiated values and the
transcript covers them, so a downgrade cannot be introduced after `hello`.

Each frame bound covers the complete frame, its four-byte length prefix included, which is the
same quantity [`crate::frame::StreamKind::max_frame_len`] bounds. A sender subtracts the prefix
to get the payload it may send.

max_attachment_frame_len.description: Maximum complete attachment frame, in bytes, length prefix included.

max_control_frame_len.description: Maximum complete control frame, in bytes, length prefix included.

max_input_frame_len.description: Maximum complete input frame, in bytes, length prefix included.

max_send_queue_bytes.description: Maximum queued bytes before the peer is resynchronised.

RecoveryBundle.description:
The versioned recovery bundle an owner keeps at a stable locator.

Enabling a new backup writer or rotating its signing key commits an updated bundle before that
writer is declared recovery-enabled.

checkpoints.description: The latest generation the owner verified for each archive.

revision.description: The bundle revision, advanced on every compare-and-swap write.

trusted_writers.description: The writers a restore may trust.

written_at_ms.description: When the owner wrote it, in UTC milliseconds.

RecoveryKit.description:
The printable and QR recovery kit.

A seed with no way to find the encrypted bundle is not a complete kit, so the kit names the
configured service origins and the stable bundle locator alongside the seed.

`Debug` is derived, and the seed redacts itself, so a kit can be logged without publishing the
owner's recovery authority.

bundle_locator.description: The stable opaque locator of the recovery bundle.

profile_version.description: The kit format and cryptographic profile version.

seed.description:
The 256-bit recovery seed. It zeroises when the kit is dropped and never appears in debug
output: it is the whole of the owner's recovery authority.

seed_checksum.description: The seed checksum, so a mistyped kit fails before it is used.

RegistrationToken.description: A provider registration token, printable ASCII without spaces. It reaches the gateway once and is never carried in a record that leaves it.

RejectionReason.description: Why an action was rejected before dispatch.

oneOf.description: Admission failed: authority, preconditions, limits or schema.
The accepted deadline passed before dispatch.
The actor or the host owner cancelled an undispatched intent.
A revocation fenced the action before dispatch.
A subject precondition no longer held in the serial dispatch path.

RelayConsumptionAck.description:
The service's answer to a consumption report.

It states what the service has recorded rather than what the report contained, so a relay
recovering from a crash learns from one exchange exactly which position to replay from.

awaiting_receipts.description:
True when the service is holding out for receipts it has not been given. The reservation
stays outstanding until they arrive or until it is settled conservatively.

bytes_recorded.description: The cumulative bytes recorded for the reservation.

next_sequence.description: The next sequence the service will accept. A relay resumes from here.

recorded_through.description: The highest sequence recorded for it, or null when none has been.

reservation_id.description: The reservation the report was about.

RelayConsumptionReceipt.description:
A relay's signed statement of what one reservation has spent.

The count is cumulative for the reservation, so a duplicate delivery of a receipt costs nothing
and a later receipt states the whole figure rather than an increment. It does not make a missing
receipt harmless: the service records receipts in order, and a relay that cannot supply the one
in between has lost the evidence for that stretch, which is settled conservatively rather than
assumed away.

bytes_consumed.description: The bytes spent from the reservation so far. Cumulative and never decreasing.

lease_revision.description: The lease revision that was in force when the count was taken.

observed_at_ms.description: When the relay took the count, in UTC milliseconds.

relay_instance_id.description: The relay instance that counted the bytes.

reservation_id.description: The reservation the bytes were spent from.

sequence.description:
The position of this receipt in that reservation's own sequence. It starts at
[`FIRST_RECEIPT_SEQUENCE`] and increases by one, so a gap is detectable and a repeat is
recognisable.

RelayConsumptionReport.description:
What a relay posts to the service to report consumption.

A report carries receipts for one reservation in ascending order. Reporting is idempotent, so a
relay that is unsure whether a report arrived sends it again rather than skipping it, and a
relay resuming after a restart replays from the last position the service acknowledged.

receipts.description: The receipts, in ascending sequence order.

RelayDirection.description: Which way a lease permits a payload to travel.

oneOf.description: Only from the source endpoint to the destination endpoint.
Both ways between the two endpoints.

RelayGrace.description:
The bounded grace a principal is inside, as the service has told this relay.

Section 17 grants a principal up to fifteen minutes or 100 MiB after exhaustion, whichever ends
first, shared across every connection of that principal. It starts at the first exhaustion
event, and reconnects, new endpoints and other regions cannot restart it: only the service knows
when the principal first exhausted its allowance, and a relay only ever receives what is left of
one grace period as a slice of it.

The slice is expressed as a raised cumulative ceiling on the same reservation, so the relay has
one number to compare its running total against whether the lease is in grace or not.

byte_ceiling.description:
The cumulative bytes this reservation may reach inside the grace. Never below the lease's
own ceiling, and above it by at most [`MAX_GRACE_BYTES`].

ends_at_ms.description: When it ends, in UTC milliseconds.

started_at_ms.description: When the principal's grace began, in UTC milliseconds.

RelayInstanceId.description: One relay instance. Stable across rotation of the key it signs receipts with.

RelayInstanceKey.description: A 32-byte Ed25519 relay instance public key. On the wire it is a CBOR byte string; in JSON it is unpadded base64url.

RelayInstanceRegistration.description:
A relay instance's registration with the service.

The instance key is generated on the relay host and never leaves it, so the service learns the
public half here and verifies every later receipt against it.

A registration is replaced rather than amended, and [`Self::replaces`] is the whole rule for
when one may replace another. Two things make that rule necessary: a registration is a signed
document, so without a revision an old one could be replayed to cancel a rotation, and a
successor that could install itself the moment its overlap opened would strand every receipt its
predecessor had signed but not yet delivered.

instance_key.description: The public half of the key this instance signs receipts with.

region.description: The deployment region this instance serves.

relay_instance_id.description: The instance identity. Stable across key rotation.

relay_url.description: The URL clients reach this instance at.

revision.description:
The revision of this registration. Strictly increasing per instance, so a registration the
instance has replaced cannot be replayed to undo the replacement. The same revision is
accepted again only for a byte-identical retry.

successor.description: The successor key and its overlap window, or null when no rotation is announced.

valid_from_ms.description: When the registration starts being valid, in UTC milliseconds.

valid_until_ms.description: When it stops being valid, in UTC milliseconds.

RelayKeySuccession.description:
A successor key and the window in which both keys are accepted.

Rotation cannot be instantaneous: receipts signed before the change are still in flight when the
new key starts signing. The overlap is that window, stated in advance and ending at a recorded
time rather than whenever somebody remembers to retire the old key.

overlap_from_ms.description: When the successor starts being accepted, in UTC milliseconds.

predecessor_retires_at_ms.description: When the key it replaces stops being accepted, in UTC milliseconds.

RelayLease.description:
A signed service capability to forward between one pair of endpoints.

This is the object section 17 requires a relay to hold before it forwards a peer payload. Every
field is inside the signature, so a relay that trusts its pinned issuer keys, and keeps the
durable state named at the top of this module, needs nothing else to decide whether a payload
may cross a boundary.

byte_ceiling.description:
The cumulative bytes this reservation may reach at the metering boundary. A refill raises
it; it never falls.

direction.description: Whether the reverse direction is permitted too.

expires_at_ms.description: When the lease stops being valid, in UTC milliseconds.

grace.description: The bounded grace this pair is inside, or null when the principal is not in grace.

issuer_key.description:
The service admission key that signs this lease. A relay accepts it only when the key is
one it pins.

lease_id.description: The lease identity. One lease covers one endpoint pair for one payer.

metering_relay_instance_id.description: The relay instance that counts the bytes. One of the two positions in the scope.

metering_role.description: Which of that instance's own boundaries takes the count.

payer_authorisation.description: Why that principal is the one billed.

relay_scope.description: The two relay positions this lease is valid at.

reservation_id.description:
The reserved block this lease spends from. It is bound for its lifetime to this lease, this
payer, this pair and this metering boundary; changing any of them takes a new reservation.

revision.description:
The revision of this lease. Strictly increasing per lease identity; a relay keeps the
highest revision it has seen and refuses anything lower, so a replaced lease cannot be
rolled back to an earlier ceiling or an earlier deadline.

RelayLeaseAck.description:
A relay's answer to a control request.

An exact retry of an installation answers with the same state and the same running figures: the
relay keeps what it has counted, so re-sending a lease can never restore a spent ceiling.

bytes_consumed.description: The cumulative bytes counted for its reservation so far.

bytes_remaining.description: The bytes still forwardable under it.

grace_remaining_ms.description:
The milliseconds of grace left, or null when the pair is not in grace. Section 17 requires
the remaining interval to be visible before the relay closes.

revision.description: The revision the relay now holds.

state.description: What the relay holds for that lease.

RelayLeaseId.description: One relay lease, covering one endpoint pair for one payer.

RelayLeaseRequest.description: What the payer's client sends to a relay's control endpoint.

oneOf.description: Install a lease, or replace an installed one with a higher revision.

lease.description:
The lease to install. Boxed because a lease is much the larger of the two requests and
an unboxed variant would make every revocation carry its size.

oneOf.description: Stop forwarding under a lease and fence traffic that is queued but not yet forwarded.

RelayLeaseRevision.description: The revision of one relay lease. Only the issuing service advances it.

RelayLeaseRevocation.description:
A service instruction to stop forwarding under a lease.

Revocation carries the revision it installs, so it orders against lease installation on one
scale: a relay that has already seen a higher revision ignores it, and a lease that arrives
afterwards at a lower revision is ignored in turn.

issued_at_ms.description: When the service issued it, in UTC milliseconds.

issuer_key.description: The service admission key that signs it.

lease_id.description: The lease to stop forwarding under.

relay_instance_id.description:
The relay instance this revocation is addressed to, so one relay's copy cannot be replayed
at another.

revision.description: The revision this revocation installs. Strictly higher than the revision it fences.

RelayLeaseState.description: What a relay holds for a lease identity after a control request.

oneOf.description: The revision is installed and forwarding.
A higher revision replaced this one.
The service revoked it.
Its deadline passed.
Its reserved bytes are spent.

RelayReceiptSequence.description: The position of one consumption receipt inside its reservation's sequence.

RelayRegion.description: The deployment region one relay instance serves.

RelayRegistrationRevision.description: The revision of one relay instance's registration. Only the instance advances it.

RelayReservationId.description: One reserved block of relay bytes. Consumption receipts are keyed by it.

RelayScope.description:
The two relay positions one lease is valid at.

This is the lease's relay scope. It names positions rather than a set of permitted instances,
because a set says which relays may forward without saying which route they are forwarding on:
a pair could then use a second relay of the set and never pass the boundary that counts. The
ingress position is where the source endpoint's payloads enter the relay tier and the egress
position is where they leave it. A single-relay route names the same instance twice, which is
the ordinary case.

egress_relay_instance_id.description: The relay instance the destination endpoint is connected to.

ingress_relay_instance_id.description: The relay instance the source endpoint is connected to.

RemoteDispatchLeaseId.description: One remote dispatch lease from the current controller generation.

RemoteSpecification.description:
A remote a repository operation reaches, and who authenticates it.

The URL is here; a credential is not, and there is no field one could travel in. What the host
records and what a diagnostic shows is this object, so a credential cannot leak through either.

credential_broker.description:
The approved credential broker that authenticates it, when the transport needs one.

Empty for a transport that needs no credential. A named broker is one the host has, and a
name it does not have is refused before anything is executed.

provider.description: The provider that serves it, as the host resolved it from the host name.

remote_name.description: The remote's name inside the repository, conventionally `origin`.

url.description: The URL, with no user information and no credential.

RemoteTransport.description:
The transports a repository operation may use.

An allowlist, because the question is not which transports Git can be talked into using (a list
nobody can close: `ext::`, `file://` to a submodule helper, a remote helper on the path) but
which ones this host validated. Everything else is refused with the reason, which is what
section 14 means by validating the transport before executing it.

oneOf.description: `https://`. The credential broker supplies the authentication.
`ssh://`, or the `user@host:path` form. The broker supplies the key.

A local path on this host, used for a clone between two directories of the same machine.

The path is an authorised source handle rather than a URL, so a `file://` URL that Git
would hand to a helper never appears.

RepositoryGeneration.description: The catalogue generation a plugin package was resolved against.

method.description: The method name. A name that is not in the registry is denied.

method_version.description: The method version. Schemas are closed for the negotiated version.

request_id.description: Correlates the response. Unique for the lifetime of one connection.

RequestId.description: A request identifier, unique for the lifetime of one connection.

RequiredAuthority.description:
What a request must present besides a valid current grant.

An empty required-rights list is not "no check". It means scoped read authority and nothing
more: a valid, unexpired, unrevoked grant for this actor that covers the named environment and
the named resource. Only reads of host and environment configuration use it.

oneOf.description: One right from the section 10 action vocabulary.

Ownership of the named resource by the verified actor: its own draft, its own attachment,
its own question or its own undispatched action.
A pairing transcript proof bound to the pinned endpoint identities.
The invitation's issuing-owner context.
A separately created voice grant, intersected with the actor's ordinary grant.
An installation or host service credential presented at a service endpoint.
The registered plugin effect's own declared rights, intersected at dispatch.
The verified originating application or helper and its caller token on private IPC.

Current issuer or delegation authority over the named grant: the actor holds the parent
grant it is delegating from, or issued the grant it is revoking. Holding a right that a
grant happens to contain never implies authority over the grant itself.

Current read authority over the subject the host resolves from the named resource, rather
than over a resource the request states. For a session subject that is `session.view` at
the session's current scope; for a host or environment subject it is the actor's current
read scope over that environment. It is a read requirement: permission to have performed
the original effect is not required, and is not sufficient either. Holding a stale
identifier is never enough.

RequiredRight.description:

WorkerLaunchSpec.description:
What the controller tells a worker to become, over the private rendezvous channel.

The job definition that started the worker carries only non-secret facts: the reservation, the
rendezvous address and the runtime directory. Everything else arrives here, after the worker
has proved which reservation it belongs to, so a creator's environment snapshot never sits in
an argument vector or an environment variable where another process could read it.

controller_generation.description: The generation that spawned this worker.

controller_public_key.description: The controller's public key, recorded so the worker can check generation tokens.

create.description: The create request the controller admitted.

display_number.description: The local alias, which also names the worker's endpoint.

environment_id.description: The environment the session belongs to.

release.description: The release string the session reports as its terminal program version.

session_id.description: The session the worker will own.

WorkerProfile.description:
How long a worker's execution context lasts.

The profile is recorded on every worker. It decides what a logout means: a desktop-bound worker
is closed with `desktop_lost` when its login-session generation ends, while a headless worker
survives logout where the platform's user service manager does.

oneOf.description: Bound to the boot identity and the current graphical login-session generation.
Bound to the boot identity and the OS user, independently of a graphical login.

WorkerReady.description: What a worker reports once its root shell is running.

dimensions.description: The geometry the shell started at.

WorkerRendezvous.description: A worker's startup claim, signed with the key it just generated.

boot_identity.description: The boot the worker started in.

process_start_identity.description:
The worker's own process identity, which the controller compares with what the launcher
reported and with the connecting peer.

reservation_id.description: The reservation this worker was started for.

signature.description: The signature over [`rendezvous_elements`].

worker_public_key.description: The public half of the worker's new per-session key.

WorkerVerifyChallenge.description: A fresh challenge sent to a worker's private endpoint.

nonce.description: Thirty-two fresh random bytes. A reused challenge proves nothing.

WorkerVerifyProof.description:
A worker's answer to a challenge.

The verifier checks the signature against the descriptor's public key **and** compares every
identity field with the descriptor. A worker that answers with a different session, epoch, boot
or process is not the worker the descriptor named.

boot_identity.description: The boot the worker is running in.

endpoint.description: The endpoint the challenge arrived on.

protocol_version.description: The protocol version the worker speaks.

signature.description: The signature over [`verify_elements`].

WorkspaceCreateParams.description:
Parameters of `workspace.preview`, which is a read `workspace.create` shares its shape with.

This is not a method of its own: `workspace.create` carries the same fields and the daemon
answers the preview from the create parameters when `preview_only` is set. One shape is a
convenience rather than a binding: a preview and a creation are two independent requests, and
a creation returns the preview it was created under, which is what a client shows.

base_change_set_id.description: The change-set version an isolated workspace materialises, when it names one.

base_revision.description: The revision an isolated workspace starts from, when it names one directly.

destination.description:
Where an isolated workspace's working tree goes.

A shared workspace names none: it is the repository's own tree.

isolation.description: How an isolated workspace is separated. Ignored for a shared one.

kind.description: Which kind it is. Explicit, with no default.

label.description: The label the user gave it.

policy.description: The inclusion policy, one decision per class.

preview_only.description:
Return the preview and create nothing.

The create interface previews first, and the preview is this method with nothing written.
It is still a mutation in the registry, because the parameters are the same object and a
caller that may not create a workspace has no business measuring one.

project_repository_id.description: The repository to make a working copy of.

preview.description: What a reviewer would see, always.

unapplied.description:
The paths the policy included that this host could not carry into the workspace.

A symbolic link, a device, a submodule's own working tree, and a path whose destination
this host could not replace. The workspace exists and is usable; what it does not hold is
named here rather than left for a reviewer to notice.

workspace.description: The workspace, or nothing when this was a preview.

WorkspaceId.description: One selected working copy and its policy.

WorkspaceKind.description:
Which kind of working copy a workspace is.

There is no default. Section 14 requires the choice to be explicit, because the two have
different concurrency and different guarantees, and a host that picked one would be choosing
for the user.

oneOf.description:
The user's own working tree, used where it is.

Dirty and untracked files stay exactly as they are. Concurrency is the limit of the tree
itself: one working tree, one index, and every session bound to this workspace sees the
other's edits. An apply to it is best-effort conflict detection rather than
compare-and-swap.

A separate working tree materialised from a named base.

The base is a revision or a change-set version, and what of the user's uncommitted work
comes with it is the explicit inclusion policy. A Git worktree implements the isolation of
working *files*; it shares repository metadata and runs under the same account, so it is not
a security sandbox. Where that matters the host uses an independent clone.

project_repository_id.description: One repository to list, or none for every repository in the environment.

retention.description: What the removal does with what the workspace holds.

retained.description: What is still held, and is waiting for the user's approval.

working_files_removed.description:
True when this workspace's own working files are gone.

Read from the filesystem rather than from what the removal did: the tree is not there any
more, whether this call removed it, an earlier one did, or the user did. A removal never
touches a *shared* workspace's tree, because that tree is the user's own, so this is
ordinarily false for one; it says false whenever the host could not establish that the
directory is absent.

workspace.description: The workspace, in the state the removal left it.

WorkspaceState.description: What state one workspace is in.

oneOf.description: It exists and can be used.
Its materialisation is still running.

The user asked for it to be removed and something it holds is retained.

A workspace reaches this state rather than disappearing when it still holds dirty content,
a pinned change set or review evidence. What is retained is listed, and the removal
finishes when the user approves it.
It is gone. The record stays so a later read says what happened rather than nothing.

WorkspaceSummary.description: One workspace, as a scoped read returns it.

base_change_set_id.description: The change-set version it materialised, when it named one.

bound_runs.description:
The automation runs bound to it that are still live.

Section 14 makes cleanup wait for every bound session *and run*. A run can hold a workspace
between two sessions or after its last one ended, so it is recorded separately and refuses
a removal in the same way.

bound_sessions.description:
The sessions bound to it that are still live.

A removal is refused while this is not empty, whatever retention policy it carries.

detail.description: Why it is in the state it is in, when it ended up there for a reason.

display_path.description: The path it was created at, for a person to read.

filesystem_identity.description:
The stable filesystem identity of its working tree, once this host has one.

Absent while the workspace is being materialised, and absent afterwards only when the
materialisation did not get as far as creating the tree. An absent identity is what refuses
a removal: this host does not delete a directory it cannot prove it created.

isolation.description: How an isolated workspace is separated, when it is one.

label.description: The label the user gave it.

policy.description: The inclusion policy it was created under.

project_repository_id.description: The repository it is a working copy of.

retained.description: What it holds that a removal would have to account for.

state.description: What state it is in.
